title: Money and unit economics
summary: Cash flow, payment terms, holds, true profit per FTD, payback, reinvestment rules, currency risk, records and a weekly cash forecast. Most profitable operators who fail run out of cash, not ideas, and this module teaches you to see the squeeze before it arrives.

lessons.title: Cash flow and payment terms
objectives: By the end you can explain why a profitable campaign can still run out of cash.
You can read common payment terms such as weekly, net 15 and net 30.
You can calculate the cash you must fund before your first payout arrives.

steps.p: A campaign can be profitable on paper and still empty your bank account. You pay the ad platform today. The network pays you weeks later. The gap between those two dates is where many growing operators get stuck, even when every number on the dashboard looks good.

d.s: Timing decides whether you survive growth

steps.say: Here's the big idea for this lesson. Profit is not cash. A campaign can look profitable on paper and still empty your bank account. Why? Because you pay the ad platform today, and the network pays you weeks later. That gap between the two dates is where a lot of growing operators get stuck, even when every number on the dashboard looks good. Timing decides whether you survive growth.

steps.h: Two ways to read the same month
steps.p: Your dashboard shows profit: what you earned minus what you spent. Your bank account shows cash: what has actually arrived minus what has actually left. Advanced operators watch both, and they plan budgets from the second one.
steps.say: Look at the two columns on screen. They describe the same month in two ways. On the left, the profit view: what you earned this month, minus what you spent. It looks healthy early, but it ignores when the money actually lands. On the right, the cash view: money that has landed, minus money that has left. That one shows the real squeeze. Advanced operators watch both, but they plan their budgets from the cash view.

steps.h: The cash cycle of one conversion
steps.p: Follow one deposit from ad to payout. Your money leaves at the first step. It only comes back at the last step. Every step in between adds days, and some steps can reduce what you are finally paid.
steps.say: Let's follow one deposit from the ad all the way to your payout. Read the steps from left to right. You fund the ad spend. The platform bills you. The network records the F T D, the first time deposit. The period closes and there's an invoice. Then a hold or review. And finally, the payout lands. Notice your money leaves at the very first step, and only comes back at the last. Every step in between adds days, and some can reduce what you're finally paid.

steps.p: Networks pay on a schedule written in your terms. "Net 15" usually means payment is due 15 days after the billing period closes. The earliest conversion in a monthly period waits the longest. Rough guide only, at the time of writing; terms differ by network, so read your own.
steps.more: Why the range? Under monthly net 15, a conversion on the last day of October is paid around 15 November, so it waits about 15 days. A conversion on 1 October waits until the same date, about 45 days. Counting both the launch day and the payout day, that is 46 days of spend you fund. When you plan cash, use the longest wait, because your spend starts on day one.

rows: Month paid 15 days after it ends
Month paid 30 days after it ends

steps.say: Networks pay on a schedule written in your terms. This table is a rough guide only, at the time of writing, and terms differ by network, so always read your own. Weekly usually means cash waits about seven to fourteen days. Monthly net fifteen means the month is paid fifteen days after it ends, so cash waits fifteen to forty five days. Why the range? The earliest conversion in the month waits the longest. Spend starts on day one, so plan with the longest wait. And new partners may face a hold, so ask.

steps.p: Before your first payout arrives, every dollar of spend comes from your own pocket. Multiply your daily spend by the number of days until the first payout. That is the minimum cash the plan needs, before any buffer.
steps.say: Here's the formula on screen. Before your first payout arrives, every dollar of spend comes out of your own pocket. So take your daily spend, multiply it by the number of days until the first payout, and that gives you the cash you must fund. That's the minimum the plan needs, and it's before any buffer. Keep this simple multiplication in mind, because we'll use it in the example next.

steps.p: Example: you start a campaign on 1 October at $300 a day. The network pays monthly, net 15. October earnings arrive around 15 November. From 1 October to 15 November, counting both days, you pay for 46 days of spend.
steps.more: Example, continued. Say the campaign runs at 30% ROI, so it earns $390 for every $300 spent. October earnings are 31 days × $390 = $12,090, paid around 15 November. By then you have spent $13,800, so you are still $1,710 behind in cash even though October made $2,790 profit on paper (31 × $90). November earnings of 30 × $390 = $11,700 land around 15 December. By that date you have spent 76 × $300 = $22,800 and received $23,790, so you are finally $990 ahead. A profitable campaign took about 11 weeks to put cash back in your account.

d.text: Example: 46 days × $300 = $13,800 spent before the first payout lands.

steps.say: Let's work an example. You start a campaign on the first of October, at three hundred dollars a day. The network pays monthly, net fifteen, so October's earnings arrive around the fifteenth of November. Counting both days, that's forty six days of spend you pay for. Forty six times three hundred dollars is thirteen thousand eight hundred dollars spent before the first payout lands. Even at thirty percent R O I, return on investment, you're still behind in cash after that first payout. In this example it took about eleven weeks for the campaign to put cash back in your account.

steps.h: The number to know before you scale
steps.p: In the example, the peak cash need is the spend that happens before the first payout. If you do not have this money, the campaign will stop for lack of cash, not for lack of results. Work this number out before you raise any budget.

If you don't have this money, the campaign stops for lack of cash, not for lack of results. So work this number out before you raise any budget.

steps.h: Ways to close the cash gap
steps.p: You cannot remove the gap, but you can shrink it or prepare for it. Each option below has a cost, so pick the ones that fit your stage and your relationship with the network.
d: Start smaller|grow spend in line with cash
Better terms|ask for weekly pay after a track record
Cash buffer|keep weeks of spend in reserve
Mix offers|some partners pay faster than others
Forecast weekly|see the squeeze before it arrives
steps.say: You can't remove the cash gap, but you can shrink it or prepare for it. Look at the cards. Start smaller, and grow spend in line with cash. Ask for better terms, like weekly pay, once you have a track record. Keep a cash buffer of a few weeks of spend. Mix offers, because some partners pay faster than others. And forecast weekly, so you see the squeeze before it arrives. Each option has a cost, so pick what fits your stage and your relationship with the network.

steps.p: These mistakes are behind most cash crunches in growing affiliate businesses. Each one has a simple fix that costs nothing but a few minutes with the forecast before you change a budget.
d: Planning from the dashboard|plan from the cash forecast
Using the shortest wait|plan with the longest wait in the period
Forgetting rejections and fees|forecast approved cash after fees
Raising budget on a good week|check the forecast before every increase
No buffer|keep weeks of spend in reserve
steps.say: These mistakes are behind most cash crunches in growing affiliate businesses. Planning from the dashboard, when you should plan from the cash forecast. Using the shortest wait, instead of the longest wait in the period. Forgetting rejections and fees, when you should forecast approved cash after fees. Raising budget on a good week without checking the forecast. And having no buffer at all. Every fix here costs nothing but a few minutes with the forecast before you change a budget.

steps.h: Do not fund tests with expensive debt
steps.p: Borrowing to fund unproven campaigns turns a normal losing test into a debt problem. Even a winning campaign needs weeks before cash returns, and interest keeps running the whole time.

d.text: Never borrow costly short-term money to fund spend you have not proven. A good campaign with a bad cash plan can still sink you.

lessons.title: Holds, reserves and clawbacks
objectives: By the end you can explain holds, reviews, reserves, thresholds and clawbacks.
You can calculate what you will actually be paid from a reported number.
You can ask a network for better terms with a clear case.

steps.p: A conversion on your dashboard is a claim, not money. It passes through review, can be rejected, can be partly held back and can even be reversed later. Advanced operators forecast with what they expect to be paid, not with what they see reported.

d.s: Every conversion passes checks before it becomes money

steps.say: Here's the big idea. Earned is not paid. A conversion on your dashboard is a claim, not money. It goes through review. It can be rejected. Part of it can be held back, and it can even be reversed later. That's why advanced operators forecast with what they expect to be paid, not with what they see reported. Every conversion passes checks before it becomes money.

steps.p: Most networks move conversions through a status path like this one. Each status has a name in your dashboard. Learn your network's names and how long each step usually takes, because that timing feeds your cash forecast.
steps.say: Follow the status path on screen, left to right. A conversion is recorded. It sits as pending. The advertiser reviews it. It's approved or rejected. Then it goes onto an invoice, and finally it's paid. Most networks use a path like this, and each status has its own name in your dashboard. Learn your network's names, and how long each step usually takes, because that timing feeds straight into your cash forecast.

steps.h: Five things that reduce or delay payouts
steps.p: These terms appear in most affiliate agreements. Find each one in your own contract. If a term is missing or vague, ask the network manager to explain it in writing before you scale.
d: Hold|first payouts delayed for new partners
Reserve|a share held back for a set period
steps.say: These five terms appear in most affiliate agreements. A hold means first payouts are delayed for new partners. A review is when the advertiser checks quality and duplicates. A reserve is a share held back for a set period. A clawback is when earnings that were approved get reversed later. And a threshold is the minimum balance before you get paid out. Find each of these in your own contract. If a term is missing or vague, ask the network manager to explain it in writing before you scale.

steps.p: Start with what the dashboard reports. Remove what the advertiser rejects. What remains is payable. Then subtract any reserve and fees to see what actually lands in your account this cycle.
steps.say: Here's the formula. Start with what the dashboard reports. Subtract what the advertiser rejects. What's left is payable. Then subtract any reserve and fees, and you get the cash that actually lands in your account this cycle. Read it across the screen: reported, minus rejected, minus reserve and fees, equals cash this cycle.

steps.p: Example: you report 100 FTDs on a $60 CPA offer. The advertiser rejects 8 as duplicates or below the baseline deposit. The network keeps a 10% rolling reserve for 90 days.
steps.more: Example, step by step. Headline value: 100 × $60 = $6,000. Approved: 92 × $60 = $5,520, so the approval rate is 92%. Reserve: 10% of $5,520 = $552, released after 90 days if no further problems appear. Paid this cycle: $5,520 − $552 = $4,968. If a wire fee of $35 applies, the cash that lands is $4,933. Your forecast should use $4,933, not $6,000. That is about 18% less than the headline.

d.text: Example: 92 × $60 = $5,520 approved. 10% reserve = $552 held. Paid now = $4,968.

With a thirty five dollar wire fee, about eighteen percent less than the headline lands.

steps.h: Work out your real approval rate
steps.p: Do this with your last full payout period. You need two numbers from the network and one from your own tracker. It takes about ten minutes and it changes every forecast you write after it.

steps.title: Pick a closed period

steps.title: Count reported and approved
steps.text: Note the total reported and how many were approved. Compare the total with your own tracker.

steps.title: Divide
steps.text: Approved ÷ reported is your approval rate. A gap with your tracker of more than a few conversions is worth a question.

steps.title: Put it in the forecast

Fourth, put it in the forecast, replacing the headline payout with cash per reported F T D. It takes about ten minutes.

steps.p: Starting rules with example thresholds; adapt them to your offers. The Budget and kill rules module counts only network-confirmed conversions, so a falling approval rate quietly raises your real CPA even when the platform dashboard looks fine.

rows: Hold spend at the current level

steps.say: Here are starting rules, with example thresholds, to adapt to your offers. When judging C P A, use network approved F T Ds only. If approval is under eighty five percent for two weeks, cap spend and review traffic quality. If rejections jump with no reasons, make no increases with that network. If a payout is over seven days late, hold spend at the current level. Remember, a falling approval rate quietly raises your real C P A, even when the platform dashboard looks fine.

steps.h: What to ask for once you have a track record
steps.p: After a few months of clean, approved traffic, you have a case. Bring your approval rate and volume to the network manager and ask for terms that shorten the cash gap. Get any change in writing.
d: A lower reserve or none at all
A shorter hold on new offers
steps.say: Once you have a few months of clean, approved traffic, you have a case to make. Bring your approval rate and volume to the network manager, and ask for terms that shorten the cash gap. Here's the checklist of what to ask for: weekly or bi-weekly payouts, a lower reserve or none at all, a shorter hold on new offers, written reasons for every rejection, and a cheaper payout method. And get any change in writing.

steps.p: Honest networks explain changes in advance and in writing. Unexplained rejections, terms that change after you have sent traffic, or payouts that keep slipping are warning signs.

d.text: If rejections spike without written reasons or payouts keep slipping, slow your spend with that network until it is resolved.

objectives: By the end you can build a simple profit and loss statement from revenue to operating profit.
You can calculate cost per FTD, overhead per FTD and true profit per FTD.

steps.h: Revenue is not what you keep
steps.p: Revenue is the top line. It is the number people like to post. What pays your team, your tools and you is what is left after ad spend and overheads. Advanced operators judge every decision by profit, not revenue.

d.b: Revenue is not what you keep
d.s: Profit after every cost is the real score

steps.say: Here's the big idea. Revenue is not what you keep. Revenue is the top line, the number people like to post. But what pays your team, your tools, and you, is what's left after ad spend and overheads. That's why advanced operators judge every decision by profit, not revenue. Profit after every cost is the real score.

steps.h: A simple profit and loss statement
steps.p: Example monthly statement for a small team. Read it from top to bottom. Each line removes a cost until you reach operating profit, the money the business made before tax.
steps.more: Example overheads: team pay $4,500, software and tracking tools $600, creative production $900, total $6,000. Tax, loan repayments and owner drawings come after this line. How tax is calculated depends on your country and your business structure, so ask a qualified accountant.
steps.say: This is an example monthly profit and loss statement for a small team. Read it from top to bottom. Revenue, the payouts earned, is forty thousand dollars. Minus ad spend of twenty eight thousand gives gross profit of twelve thousand. Minus overheads, team, tools and creatives, of six thousand, gives operating profit of six thousand dollars. That's what the business made before tax. How tax is calculated depends on your country and business structure, so ask a qualified accountant.

steps.p: Write this formula at the top of your monthly report. If you only track the first two terms, you will think you are doing better than you are, and you will scale overheads you cannot afford.
steps.say: Here's the formula to write at the top of your monthly report. Revenue, minus ad spend, minus overheads, equals operating profit. Why does this matter? If you only track the first two terms, you'll think you're doing better than you are. And then you'll scale overheads you can't afford.

steps.p: The same example as a monthly sheet. Add one row for approved FTDs and divide operating profit by it. That single cell, true profit per FTD, is the number this lesson is about.

One row for approved F T Ds, first time deposits, eight hundred in this example. Then divide operating profit by it. Six thousand dollars divided by eight hundred is seven dollars fifty. That single highlighted cell, true profit per F T D, is the number this whole lesson is about.

steps.h: Three margins from the same month
steps.p: Illustration of the example. Gross margin is 30% ($12,000 ÷ $40,000). Operating margin is 15% ($6,000 ÷ $40,000). Half the gross profit went to running the business, which is normal once you have a team.

steps.p: Unit economics means looking at one customer at a time. These four numbers tell you whether each FTD makes money and how long it takes, which is what decides whether scaling is safe.
d: CAC|what one FTD costs you to acquire
LTV|what one FTD earns you over its life
Contribution|what one FTD leaves after its costs
steps.say: Unit economics means looking at one customer at a time. Here are the four words to know. C A C, customer acquisition cost, is what one F T D costs you to acquire. L T V, lifetime value, is what one F T D earns you over its life. Payback is the time until earnings cover C A C. And contribution is what one F T D leaves after its costs. Together they tell you whether each F T D makes money and how long it takes, which decides whether scaling is safe.

steps.p: Example: at a $50 CPA, $40,000 revenue means 800 FTDs. Spend of $28,000 ÷ 800 = $35 per FTD. Overheads of $6,000 ÷ 800 = $7.50 per FTD.
steps.more: Example, check the maths: $7.50 × 800 FTDs = $6,000, the same operating profit as the statement. Notice that the media margin looked like $15 per FTD ($50 − $35). Overheads took half of it. This is why a campaign that "makes $15 per FTD" may only add $7.50 to the business. When you set target CPAs, include overhead per FTD or your targets will be too generous.

d.text: Example: $50 payout − $35 media − $7.50 overhead = $7.50 true profit per FTD.

Spend of twenty eight thousand divided by eight hundred is thirty five dollars per F T D. Overheads of six thousand divided by eight hundred is seven dollars fifty per F T D. So fifty, minus thirty five, minus seven fifty, leaves seven dollars fifty of true profit. Notice the media margin looked like fifteen dollars, but overheads took half of it. So when you set target C P As, include overhead per F T D.

steps.h: When is an FTD paid back?
steps.p: With CPA you are paid once, so payback is the payout date. With RevShare you are paid a share of the customer's value each month, so you must count the months until the running total covers what you paid.
steps.say: When is an F T D paid back? Look at the formula. When your cumulative earnings per F T D are greater than or equal to your cost per F T D, it's paid back. With C P A you're paid once, so payback is simply the payout date. With RevShare you're paid a share of the customer's value each month, so you count the months until the running total covers what you paid.

steps.p: Example: cost per FTD is $35. On a RevShare deal, the average FTD earns you the commissions below each month. Add them up month by month and find when the running total passes $35.
steps.say: Here's a RevShare example. Your cost per F T D is thirty five dollars. Look at the table. In month one the average F T D earns you twenty four dollars, so the running total is twenty four, which doesn't cover thirty five. In month two it earns twelve more, so the running total is thirty six. That passes thirty five. After that, the months add eight, six, five and four dollars, reaching fifty nine dollars by month six.

steps.p: In the example the running total passes the $35 cost in month two. Until then, each new FTD is a cash cost to you. The longer the payback, the more cash you need to keep scaling.

d.label: payback period on a $35 FTD
d.note: Example. Average figures; real cohorts vary.

steps.say: So the payback period in this example is two months on a thirty five dollar F T D. Until then, each new F T D is a cash cost to you. And remember, these are average figures, and real cohorts vary. The longer the payback, the more cash you need to keep scaling.

steps.h: CPA or RevShare for the same FTD
steps.p: Example: the same FTD could earn a $50 CPA or the RevShare stream above. Neither is always better. The choice depends on your cash, your trust in the advertiser and how well you retain customers.

items: No upside if the customer stays
No risk if the customer leaves

b.title: RevShare
items: Risk from churn and term changes

On the right, RevShare: fifty nine dollars over six months in this example, so a twenty four dollar margin, but slower. There's upside if retention is strong, and risk from churn and term changes. steps.p: Each of these mistakes makes the business look more profitable than it is, which leads to targets that are too generous and scaling that loses money. The fixes all come from this lesson.

Ignoring overheads|add overhead per FTD to targets
RevShare on 1-2 months of data|wait for cohort months

steps.p: Starting rules to adapt. Example: payout $50 at 90% approval gives a $45 break-even. With a $28 target, 1.5 × $28 = $42, the lower of the two, so you kill at a CPA above $42 once spend reaches 3 × target, as in the Budget and kill rules module.

rows: Below break-even minus overhead per FTD
Only if payback fits the cash you hold

steps.say: These starting rules turn profit into a kill line. Break even C P A is payout times approval rate. So a fifty dollar payout at ninety percent approval gives forty five dollars. With a twenty eight dollar target, one point five times is forty two dollars, the lower of the two. So you kill at a C P A above forty two dollars once spend reaches three times target, as in the Budget and kill rules module.

objectives: By the end you can split profit into clear buckets before spending it.
You can calculate a safe daily spend ceiling from cleared cash.
You can write reinvestment rules that protect the business in a bad month.

steps.h: Every profit dollar needs a job
steps.p: When profit lands, the temptation is to throw it all back into ads. Operators who last decide in advance where each part of the profit goes. That one habit separates a business from a lucky streak.

d.b: Every profit dollar needs a job
d.s: Decide the split before the money arrives

steps.say: Here's the big idea. Every profit dollar needs a job. When profit lands, the temptation is to throw all of it back into ads. Operators who last decide in advance where each part of the profit goes. That one habit separates a business from a lucky streak. So decide the split before the money arrives.

steps.p: Most operators use some version of these buckets. The names matter less than the rule that money moves into them as soon as a payout is confirmed, before any spending decision is made.
d: Tax reserve|set aside for what you will owe
Cash buffer|covers holds, delays and bad months
Team bonus|optional, tied to clear results
steps.say: Most operators use some version of these buckets. A tax reserve, set aside for what you'll owe. A cash buffer, which covers holds, delays and bad months. Reinvest, to fund tests and careful scaling. Owner pay, a planned, regular amount. And an optional team bonus, tied to clear results. The names matter less than the rule: money moves into these buckets as soon as a payout is confirmed, before any spending decision is made.

steps.p: Illustration only. The tax percentage is a placeholder, not advice; your real figure depends on your country and structure, so ask an accountant. The point is that every dollar is assigned before you spend any of it.
steps.say: Here's an illustration of splitting six thousand dollars of profit. Reinvest thirty percent, that's one thousand eight hundred. Tax reserve twenty five percent, one thousand five hundred. Owner pay twenty five percent, one thousand five hundred. And cash buffer twenty percent, one thousand two hundred. The tax percentage is a placeholder, not advice. Your real figure depends on your country and structure, so ask an accountant. The point is that every dollar is assigned before you spend any of it.

steps.p: Your spend ceiling comes from cleared cash and your cash cycle, not from how good the campaign looks. Divide the cash you can commit by the days until the next payout lands.
steps.say: Here's how to find your safe daily spend ceiling. Look at the formula. Take your committable cash, divide it by the days until your next payout, and that's your maximum daily spend. Notice what's not in the formula: how good the campaign looks. Your ceiling comes from cleared cash and your cash cycle.

steps.p: Example: you have $9,000 in cleared cash. Your cash cycle to the next payout is 45 days. You keep 20% of cash as a buffer that is never committed to spend.
steps.more: Example, why not $200 a day? $9,000 ÷ 45 = $200 would commit every dollar you have. One delayed payout or a 10% rejection would leave you unable to pay for ads or the team. With a 20% buffer the ceiling is $160 a day. If the network moves you to weekly payouts, the cycle might fall to about 14 days and the same $7,200 supports roughly $514 a day. Better terms can raise your ceiling more than extra profit does.

d.text: Example: $9,000 × 80% = $7,200 committable. $7,200 ÷ 45 days = $160 a day ceiling.

steps.say: Let's work an example. You have nine thousand dollars in cleared cash. Your cycle to the next payout is forty five days. And you keep twenty percent as a buffer you never commit. So nine thousand times eighty percent is seven thousand two hundred committable, and divided by forty five days, that's a ceiling of one hundred and sixty dollars a day. Why not two hundred? That would commit every dollar, and one delayed payout could leave you stuck. And if the network moved you to weekly payouts, the same cash could support far more. Better terms can raise your ceiling more than extra profit does.

steps.p: This is the most the example business should spend per day across all campaigns until more cash lands. If a winning campaign wants more, the money must come from pausing a weaker one, not from the buffer.
steps.say: So the ceiling from the example is one hundred and sixty dollars a day, with nine thousand dollars cash, a twenty percent buffer and a forty five day cycle. That's the most the business should spend per day, across all campaigns, until more cash lands. If a winning campaign wants more, the money has to come from pausing a weaker one, not from the buffer.

steps.p: Do this the day a payout lands, before you touch any budget. The order matters: confirm, split, move, then set the ceiling. Doing it in that order removes the temptation to spend the whole payout on ads.

steps.h: The scaling loop with a cash check
steps.p: This loop adds one step to normal scaling: a cash check before each increase. It slows growth a little and removes the most common way profitable operators fail, which is running out of cash mid-scale.

steps.p: Write rules like these down and agree them with any partner before money arrives. Rules made in advance are much easier to follow than decisions made when you are excited or worried.

A bad month cannot sink you

steps.say: Here are reinvestment rules that protect you, with the reason for each. Reinvest only cleared payouts, because pending money can be rejected. Cap tests at a set percentage of profit, so your tuition stays limited. Set a monthly stop loss, so a bad month can't sink you. Keep a buffer of one month of overheads plus float, to survive a late payout. And pay the owner on a fixed date, so there are no raids on ad money. Write rules like these down and agree them with any partner before money arrives.

exam.why: Running total: $15, $25, $33, $39, $44. Month 4 reaches $39, still $1 short; month 5 passes $40.

exam.q: You have $15,000 cleared cash, keep a 20% buffer, and the next payout is 40 days away. A winning campaign wants $350 a day. What do you do?
options: Run $350 a day from the buffer
Cap total spend near $300 a day or fund the winner by pausing weaker campaigns
exam.why: $15,000 × 80% ÷ 40 = $300 a day ceiling. Extra spend must come from reallocating, not the buffer.

exam.q: Forecast: cash now $6,000, payouts landing next week $2,500, spend and overheads $2,600, buffer $2,000. A +20% step adds $350 next week, and the ad set has 4 network-confirmed FTDs at 0.7 × target, last changed 3 days ago. What do you do?
options: Increase: the ad rule passes and cash stays at $5,550, above the buffer
Hold: never scale in the first month
Increase by 50% because CPA is so low
Cut spend: the forecast is below the buffer
exam.why: $6,000 + $2,500 − $2,600 − $350 = $5,550, well above $2,000, and the ad set meets the +20% rule (3+ confirmed FTDs, CPA ≤ 0.8 × target, 48+ hours since the last change).

exam.q: Ads are billed in dollars to a local card and payouts arrive in USDT a month later. What is the main risk?
options: No risk if ROI is positive
Currency and timing mismatch moving your real margin
exam.why: Costs and income sit in different currencies on different dates, so rate moves change real margin.

exam.q: A teammate says crypto payouts are not taxable so records are not needed. What is the right answer?
options: Convert everything to cash first to avoid tax
Crypto income is usually taxable; keep records and ask a qualified accountant
exam.why: In most countries crypto earned is income. Keep records and get local professional advice.
